_help: Troubleshooting scenarios. Each has id, title, summary, situation, observations (list), steps (each with kind, prompt, choices (4), answer letter, explanation), takeaways (list), safety (optional), applies (optional), refs (optional).

scenarios.title: High room temperature alarm
scenarios.summary: Site reports a high temperature alarm on a perimeter DX unit.
scenarios.situation: You arrive at a small data center. The site contact says a **High Return Air Temperature** alarm started about an hour ago on one of three DX perimeter units.
observations: The iCOM display shows the alarm and 100% cooling demand.
The room feels warm near that unit.
No work was done recently, according to the site.

steps.prompt: What should you do first?
choices: Verify the actual temperature with your own instrument and review active alarms and the event log
Turn off the other two units to isolate the problem
steps.explanation: Confirm the condition is real and gather information. The event log may show an earlier alarm (for example high head pressure) that explains the high temperature.

steps.prompt: The event log shows the compressor stopped on a high head pressure alarm 70 minutes ago. Which information is most useful next?
choices: Condenser fan status, condenser coil condition and outdoor conditions
steps.explanation: High head pressure points to the heat rejection side. Check the outdoor condenser: fans running, coil clean, nothing blocking airflow, speed control working.

steps.prompt: You find one of two condenser fans not running and the coil partly blocked with cottonwood. What is the right course of action?
choices: With power locked out, diagnose the fan (power, control, capacitor/motor), clean the coil per the manual, then reset the HP switch and verify pressures
Reset the HP switch and leave
Spray water on the condenser while it runs and leave
steps.explanation: Fix the causes, then reset the safety and verify head pressure and cooling are normal. Document findings and recommend more frequent coil cleaning if cottonwood is seasonal.

takeaways: A high temperature alarm is often a consequence - look for the first alarm in the log.
High head pressure usually means a heat rejection problem.
Fix the cause before resetting a safety.
scenarios.safety: Lock out the condenser before working on fans or cleaning the coil. Never bypass the high-pressure switch.
scenarios.applies: Air-cooled DX units (e.g. Liebert DS, PDX with outdoor condenser)

scenarios.title: Compressor will not start
scenarios.summary: Cooling demand present, compressor does nothing.
scenarios.situation: A unit shows cooling demand, the fans are running, but the compressor is not running. There is no humming or clicking from the compressor.
observations: iCOM shows the compressor is called but not running.
No high- or low-pressure alarm is active.
The unit was running normally yesterday.

steps.prompt: Which check comes first?
choices: Check alarms/lockouts and whether the control circuit is energizing the compressor contactor coil
steps.explanation: Start with the control side: is the controller calling, is a safety or timer holding the compressor off, and does the contactor coil have voltage?

steps.prompt: The contactor is pulled in. You measure correct voltage on the line side, but zero volts on one leg of the load side. What does this indicate?
choices: Failed contactor contacts on that leg
steps.explanation: With the contactor closed, line and load sides should match. A missing leg on the load side means a burned contact. (Measured with proper PPE and procedures.)

steps.prompt: After replacing the contactor (with power locked out), what else should you investigate?
choices: Why the contacts burned - short cycling, low voltage, loose connections or high compressor amps
steps.explanation: Contacts fail from excessive cycling, arcing from loose connections, or overcurrent. Check the compressor's running amps and voltage after restart.

takeaways: Check controls, safeties and power before condemning a compressor.
Line vs load voltage across a closed contactor quickly identifies failed contacts.
Always look for the root cause.
scenarios.safety: Measurements on energized circuits require qualification and proper PPE. Lock out before replacing components.

scenarios.title: Compressor runs but cooling is poor
scenarios.summary: Compressor is on, but the room won't come down.
scenarios.situation: A DX unit's compressor is running continuously but supply air is only a little cooler than return air. The room is slowly warming.
observations: Filters were changed last month.
Indoor fans are running at normal speed.
The unit has a digital scroll compressor.

steps.prompt: What information will best narrow down the problem?
choices: Suction and discharge pressures, superheat/subcooling, compressor amps and the digital solenoid state
steps.explanation: Pressures, temperatures and amps tell you whether the compressor is pumping and whether the evaporator is fed. On a digital scroll, also check whether the controller is loading it.

steps.prompt: Suction and discharge pressures are nearly equal, amps are low, and the controller shows 100% compressor demand. What is a likely cause?
choices: Compressor held unloaded (digital solenoid stuck energized/valve stuck) or compressor not pumping
steps.explanation: On a digital scroll, energized solenoid = unloaded. If it stays unloaded at full demand, the compressor won't pump. Reverse rotation or internal failure can look similar - verify with the manual's procedure.

steps.prompt: How should you confirm?
choices: Check the controller output and solenoid coil voltage per the wiring diagram, then follow the unit manual's digital solenoid test procedure
steps.explanation: Confirm whether the coil is being energized when it shouldn't be (control issue) or the valve is stuck (mechanical). Liebert manuals have a section on digital scroll unloading solenoids.

takeaways: A running compressor isn't necessarily a pumping compressor.
Digital scroll: energized = unloaded, de-energized = loaded (Copeland design; confirm per unit).
Use pressures and amps together.
scenarios.safety: Refrigerant circuit work requires EPA 608 certification.
scenarios.applies: Units with digital scroll compressors (e.g. Liebert DS, DSE)

scenarios.title: Condenser fan not operating
scenarios.summary: Outdoor condenser fan is stopped in summer.
scenarios.situation: On a hot day, a technician notices an air-cooled unit's outdoor condenser fan is not turning, while the compressor is running and head pressure is climbing.
observations: Outdoor temperature is 95 F.
Other units' condensers are running.
The fan blade turns freely by hand with power locked out.

steps.prompt: What should be checked first (following safety procedures)?
choices: Power and fuses/breaker to the fan, and the fan control signal/speed controller
steps.explanation: Confirm the fan is being powered and commanded. A blown fuse, tripped breaker or failed speed controller is common.

steps.prompt: Voltage is present at the single-phase fan motor and it hums but does not turn. What is the most likely component?
steps.explanation: A hum with correct voltage and a free-turning blade suggests a failed capacitor. Discharge and test it against its rating before replacing.

steps.prompt: After replacing the capacitor, what should you verify?
choices: Fan amps, rotation direction, head pressure returning to normal and no alarms
That the HP switch is jumpered
steps.explanation: Confirm the repair restored normal operation and that head pressure and cooling are back to normal.

takeaways: No condenser airflow = rising head pressure.
Check power and control before the motor.
A humming PSC motor often has a bad capacitor.
scenarios.safety: Lock out the condenser and verify zero energy before touching the fan or discharging the capacitor. Never try to start a fan by hand.

scenarios.title: Evaporator airflow is restricted
scenarios.summary: Loss of airflow and low suction pressure on a perimeter unit.
scenarios.situation: A unit has a **Clogged Filters** warning and later a **Low Suction Pressure** alarm. The site skipped the last scheduled PM.
observations: Supply airflow feels weak.
The evaporator coil has frost on the lower section.

steps.prompt: What is the most likely cause to address first?
choices: Dirty filters (and possibly a dirty coil) restricting airflow
steps.explanation: Reduced airflow lowers the heat delivered to the coil, so suction pressure and coil temperature drop and frost forms.

steps.prompt: How should the iced coil be handled?
choices: Shut off cooling, let the coil defrost completely (fans can run if appropriate), replace filters, then restart and verify
Chip the ice off with a screwdriver
Run the compressor to melt it
steps.explanation: Never damage the coil. Let it defrost and correct the airflow before restarting cooling.

steps.prompt: After restart, what confirms the problem is fixed?
choices: Normal airflow, suction pressure/superheat in range, no frost, and alarms cleared
Supply air is colder than ever
steps.explanation: Verify with readings. If suction remains low with clean filters, investigate charge, metering and fans.

takeaways: Airflow problems can look like refrigeration problems.
Fix the cause of ice, don't just remove it.
Regular filter PM prevents this.

scenarios.title: High head pressure on a water-cooled unit
scenarios.summary: Repeated high head pressure trips on a water-cooled DX unit.
scenarios.situation: A water-cooled DX unit trips its high-pressure switch several times a day. The building engineer recently worked on the cooling tower loop.
observations: Condenser water supply temperature looks normal.
The water regulating valve seems to be barely open.

steps.prompt: Which information is most useful first?
choices: Condenser water flow and pressure drop, isolation valve positions, strainers, and the regulating valve operation
steps.explanation: Recent work on the loop and a barely open valve point to water-side flow. Check valves, strainers and the regulating valve.

steps.prompt: An isolation valve was left partly closed after the tower work. What should you do?
choices: Coordinate with the building engineer to open it fully, then verify head pressure and reset the HP switch
steps.explanation: Restoring flow fixes the cause. Coordinate with the site before changing building systems.

steps.prompt: Head pressure is now normal. What else should you do?
choices: Document the cause and readings, and recommend the site check valve positions after loop work
steps.explanation: Good documentation prevents repeat calls and helps the site.

takeaways: Water-cooled head pressure depends on water flow and temperature.
Ask about recent work on connected systems.

scenarios.title: Low suction pressure
scenarios.situation: A DX unit trips on low suction pressure. Filters and airflow have been checked and are fine.
observations: Superheat is high.
Subcooling is low.
There is an oily stain on a flare fitting near the TXV.

steps.prompt: What do high superheat, low subcooling and an oily fitting suggest?
choices: Low refrigerant charge due to a leak
steps.explanation: This is the classic undercharge pattern, and the oil stain suggests where the leak is.

steps.prompt: What is the right approach?
choices: A certified technician leak checks to confirm, repairs the leak, replaces the drier if opened, evacuates and charges to specification
steps.explanation: Repair the leak, then charge properly. Topping off wastes refrigerant, may violate EPA rules and the problem returns.

steps.prompt: If there were no leak and readings showed high subcooling with high superheat, what would you suspect instead?
choices: A restriction in the liquid line or metering device (e.g. clogged drier or failing TXV)
steps.explanation: Liquid backing up (high subcooling) while the evaporator is starved (high superheat) points to a restriction between the condenser and evaporator.

takeaways: Use superheat AND subcooling together.
Low charge means a leak - find it.
Restrictions show high subcooling + high superheat.
scenarios.safety: Only EPA 608 certified technicians may open the circuit, recover or charge refrigerant.

scenarios.title: Water leaking from the unit
scenarios.summary: Water-under-floor alarm near a perimeter unit.
scenarios.situation: A **Water Under Floor** alarm activates near a downflow unit with a humidifier and a condensate pump.
observations: Water is pooling under the unit.
The condensate pump reservoir is full.

steps.prompt: What should you do first?
choices: Make the area safe (electrical hazard), and identify the water source
Turn off all units in the room
steps.explanation: Water and electricity are a dangerous combination. Assess and control hazards, then trace the source.

steps.prompt: The pump reservoir is full and the pump is not running. What do you check?
choices: Pump power, float switch, pump motor and discharge line (blocked or check valve stuck)
steps.explanation: Work through the pump circuit and its discharge path. A clogged discharge line or stuck float is common.

steps.prompt: After repair, what helps prevent a repeat?
choices: Verify the high-water safety works, clean the drain pan/trap and add pump testing to PM
steps.explanation: A working high-water switch can stop cooling/humidification before overflow. Regular tests catch failing pumps.

takeaways: Most water leaks come from drains, pumps and humidifiers.
Test condensate pumps and high-water safeties at PM.
scenarios.safety: De-energize equipment in wet areas as required before working. Follow site procedures.

scenarios.title: Humidity above setpoint
scenarios.summary: Room RH is high and won't come down.
scenarios.situation: Room humidity has been 10-15% RH above setpoint for two days. Units report they are dehumidifying.
observations: Construction crews have been propping a room door open.
Units' reheat is running a lot.

steps.prompt: What should you verify first?
choices: The humidity reading with a calibrated instrument
steps.explanation: Make sure the sensor is right before chasing the problem.

steps.prompt: Readings are correct and the units' coils are cold. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Moisture entering the room through the propped-open door (infiltration)
steps.explanation: Outside air carries moisture. Precision units are mostly sized for sensible loads and can be overwhelmed by infiltration.

steps.prompt: What is the best action?
choices: Inform the site so the door is kept closed, and monitor recovery
steps.explanation: Fix the source. Changing setpoints won't solve infiltration.

takeaways: Verify sensors first.
Check for moisture sources outside the units.

scenarios.title: Temperature sensor reading seems wrong
scenarios.summary: Display says the room is cool but it's hot.
scenarios.situation: The site says the room is hot. The unit's display shows a return temperature of 68 F and 0% cooling demand.
observations: Your calibrated thermometer reads 82 F at the unit's return.
The sensor is mounted near the return opening.

steps.prompt: What is the most likely problem?
choices: The return temperature sensor (or its wiring/offset) is reporting incorrectly
steps.explanation: The controller isn't calling for cooling because it believes the room is cool. The sensor reading is the issue.

steps.prompt: What should you check before replacing the sensor?
choices: Wiring and connectors, the controller's calibration offset setting, and whether the unit is controlling from a different sensor
steps.explanation: A wrong offset or the wrong control sensor selection can look like a failed sensor.

steps.prompt: After correcting the issue, how do you confirm?
choices: Compare the displayed reading with your calibrated instrument and confirm cooling demand responds
steps.explanation: Verify the reading agrees and the unit responds correctly.

takeaways: Controllers act on what sensors tell them.
Check wiring, offsets and sensor selection before replacing parts.

scenarios.title: Multiple alarms at once
scenarios.summary: A burst of alarms after a power blip.
scenarios.situation: After a brief utility outage, a unit shows several alarms: Loss of Power, High Temperature, Compressor Low Pressure, and Humidifier Problem.
observations: The unit is now running but one compressor is locked out.
The site's generator transferred during the event.

steps.prompt: How should you approach this?
choices: Review the event log in time order to find the first alarm, then work through consequences
steps.explanation: One event can cause many alarms. The sequence shows cause and effect.

steps.prompt: Which power-related checks make sense?
choices: Phase voltages and rotation, phase monitor status, and auto-restart settings
steps.explanation: Power transfers can cause phase loss or imbalance. Check incoming power and how the unit restarted.

steps.prompt: Power is normal. What next for the locked-out compressor?
choices: Check the LP alarm cause (e.g. cold-start low pressure), reset per the manual, and watch it run through a full cycle
steps.explanation: A lockout after a power event may be a one-time trip, but verify by watching pressures on restart.

takeaways: Use the event log to separate root cause from consequences.
After power events, check incoming power and restart behavior.

scenarios.title: iCOM reports an abnormal condition
scenarios.summary: An unfamiliar alarm text appears on iCOM.
scenarios.situation: The iCOM display shows an alarm you have not seen before on this unit model.
observations: The unit is still cooling.
You have a phone with internet access.

steps.prompt: What should you do?
choices: Look up the alarm in the iCOM/unit manual for this model and firmware, and record the exact alarm text and time
steps.explanation: Alarm names and meanings are model and firmware specific. Use the correct documentation.

steps.prompt: What additional information helps?
choices: Event log, current operating readings, and any related warnings
steps.explanation: Context from logs and readings helps confirm the alarm is real and points toward the cause.

steps.prompt: The manual's instructions require work you aren't trained for. What do you do?
choices: Make the unit safe, document, and escalate to a qualified technician or technical support
steps.explanation: Escalating is the professional choice.

takeaways: Never guess an alarm's meaning - look it up for the model.
Record exact text, time, and readings.

scenarios.title: Condensate pump failure
scenarios.summary: High-water alarm on a ceiling-mounted unit.
scenarios.situation: A ceiling-mounted small-room unit shows a high water / condensate alarm and has stopped cooling.
observations: Ceiling tile below the unit is stained.
The unit's condensate pump is quiet.

steps.prompt: Why did the unit stop cooling?
choices: A high-water safety (float switch) likely stopped cooling to prevent overflow
steps.explanation: Many units interlock a high-water switch to shut down cooling before the pan overflows.

steps.prompt: What should be checked?
choices: Pump power, pump float, pump motor, and whether the discharge line is clogged
steps.explanation: Trace the pump circuit and discharge path.

steps.prompt: After repair, what should you do?
choices: Test by adding water, confirm the safety resets and cooling restarts, and report the ceiling damage
steps.explanation: Functional testing confirms the repair; reporting damage informs the site.

takeaways: High-water safeties protect the space - they stop cooling by design.
Check the pump and its discharge line.
scenarios.applies: Ceiling-mounted units such as Liebert Mini-Mate2 with condensate pump option

scenarios.title: Dirty air filters during PM
scenarios.summary: Routine PM finds very dirty filters.
scenarios.situation: During a scheduled PM you find the filters heavily loaded with dust. No filter alarm has appeared.
observations: The filter clog switch tubing is cracked.
Filters were last changed three months ago.

steps.prompt: Why might the filter alarm not have appeared?
choices: The cracked sensing tube prevents the differential pressure switch from sensing the pressure drop
steps.explanation: A filter clog switch measures pressure difference across the filters through tubes. A leak in the tubing defeats it.

steps.prompt: What should you do?
choices: Replace the filters, repair/replace the tubing, test the switch, and document
steps.explanation: Fix both the filters and the failed monitoring.

steps.prompt: What recommendation might you make?
choices: Shorten the filter change interval if the space is dusty
steps.explanation: Match PM intervals to conditions.

takeaways: Alarms are only as good as their sensors.
Inspect sensing devices during PM.
